headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from browser-based PDF processing feeding a networked support bot; no direct shared-channel evidence, so interaction is inferred.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: pdf.js can render attacker-controlled PDF content in a browser-based workflow, and rasa can ingest dialogue/content from external channels. No shared channel is documented, but if PDF text is copied or forwarded into rasa, prompt-like instructions could be relayed. The pairwise pathway is inferred from both profiles, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF PDF-derived text is copied into rasa conversations or training data
IF rasa treats imported text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a manual copy-paste review step before sending PDF text to rasa
Prefix imported PDF excerpts as untrusted content
Disable any automation that forwards document text into chat flows
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to document-derived messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js touches PDF documents locally, while rasa has allowlisted network egress and multiple external API surfaces. If PDF contents include sensitive data and are forwarded into rasa channels, they can leave the local document-processing boundary. The profiles do not show a shared workspace, so this is inferred rather than directly evidenced.
conditions: IF PDF documents contain sensitive personal or business data
IF those contents are sent through rasa to an external channel or integration
mitigations: Restrict rasa inputs to redacted excerpts only
Review outbound integrations and disable unnecessary API connectors
Use a local-only staging bot for document-derived text
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction before any outbound send

C_capability_conflict.rationale: pdf.js supports multiple instances and writes only PDF files, while rasa does not support multiple instances and has allowlisted egress plus chat API integrations. There is no documented shared mutable resource, so direct write-write conflict is not established. The main risk is operational contention if both are orchestrated over the same workflow, which appears unusual.
conditions: IF both agents are wired to the same mutable workspace or queue
IF the orchestrator lacks locking around shared artifacts
mitigations: Separate their working directories
Serialize access to any shared queue or file
Avoid concurrent writes to the same artifact
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js can extract or display document text, and rasa is a dialogue system that may act on user-facing content. If pdf.js output is forwarded into rasa without verification, rasa can repeat or operationalize incorrect extracted text. No evidence shows an explicit verification step, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF pdf.js-extracted text is used as rasa input
IF rasa responses are generated without human verification of the extracted text
mitigations: Require human review of extracted text before chatbot use
Mark PDF-derived facts as unverified in prompts
Limit rasa to summarization rather than action-taking
requires-engineering: add validation against source PDFs

E_compliance.rationale: pdf.js processes PDF documents locally and does not request secrets or OAuth scopes, while rasa can send data through external messaging APIs. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is visible: if regulated data is routed from pdf.js into rasa integrations, logging and retention may diverge. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from the pair.
conditions: IF regulated data from PDFs is routed into rasa-connected channels
IF those channels retain or log messages longer than the source workflow expects
mitigations: Review retention settings on each rasa connector
Avoid sending regulated PDFs into chat integrations
Document a deletion workflow for forwarded document text
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion policies across systems
